Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the outstretched hand is a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise: a normal film does not clear it, so a thumb spica now and repeat films in about 2 weeks, or MRI now Night numbness of the thumb to the radial ring finger, eased by shaking, thenar skin spared: carpal tunnel syndrome; a night splint, and release for thenar atrophy Radial styloid pain with a positive Finkelstein test: de Quervain tenosynovitis (de Quervain tendinopathy), clinical; no imaging; a thumb spica splint and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) first

What it is Wrist or hand pain, or hand numbness, in an adult Sort by Where the tenderness sits (snuffbox, radial styloid, thumb base) and which skin is numb (median, ulnar, radial, a root) Hands off Thumb base osteoarthritis: Osteoarthritis; a hot, swollen wrist: Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult Osteoarthritis Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult

Missed proximal pole fractureSnuffbox tenderness, normal first film If a scaphoid fracture is possible, choose immobilize now; never send home unsplinted. Why cast on suspicionRetrograde blood supplyThe scaphoid is fed from its distal end, so a fracture cuts off the proximal pole: a missed one may die (avascular necrosis) or fail to heal (nonunion), and the proximal pole fares worst. Pancoast tumorHand muscle atrophy with shoulder pain and Horner syndrome: a lung apex tumor on the lower trunk (C8 to T1) Acute carpal tunnel syndromeMedian numbness right after a wrist injury: a lunate dislocation

red flags and when to image · acute pain with no red flags · inflammatory back pain and spondyloarthritisIs there a red flag or a neurologic deficit, and does the pain improve when the patient moves?

Acute low back pain, no red flag, normal neurologic exam: no imaging; an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or acetaminophen, and stay active Why no imagingWhy no imagingDisc herniations and bulges are common in people without symptoms, so an early scan mostly finds lesions unrelated to the pain; up to 85% of patients recover without surgery within 6 weeks whatever the cause. A history of cancer, fever or injection drug use, or a bladder or saddle change, means imaging even when the neurologic exam is normal Night pain that eases on getting up is inflammatory; night pain that no position or analgesic relieves, with a cancer history or weight loss, points to malignancy

What it is Usually mechanical; a few cases are infection, inflammation, cancer or fracture Sort by Red flags and the neurologic exam, then how the pain answers rest and movement Hands off A fragility fracture: Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment; anterior uveitis: The Red Eye; buttock pain from the hip or piriformis: Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment The Red Eye Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness

Cauda equina syndromeUrinary retention or incontinence, saddle anesthesia, sciatica on one side or both, lost anal tone and ankle reflexes If the bladder or the saddle is involved, choose emergent MRI and surgical decompression. Spinal cord compressionUpper motor neuron signs: hyperreflexia (reflexes may be low at first when the onset is acute), an extensor plantar response, a sensory level If cancer is known or suspected, choose dexamethasone first, then emergent MRI of the whole spine. Spinal epidural abscessFever, focal spinal tenderness and neurologic signs after injection drug use or bacteremia If fever comes with a neurologic sign, choose MRI and blood cultures. Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysmOlder smoker; sudden back pain with syncope or hypotension; a pulsatile mass If the patient is unstable, choose straight to surgery.

Low back pain, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Lumbosacral strain After lifting; paraspinal tenderness; a symmetric, belt-like ache Acute, settles within weeks; normal neurologic exam, negative straight-leg raise Lumbar radiculopathy from a disc Pain shooting below the knee; positive straight-leg raise Sudden onset; most settle within 6 weeks; imaging (MRI) for a deficit or pain past 6 weeks (the ladder, rung 2) Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication) Older; buttock and leg pain on walking or standing Chronic; eased by sitting or leaning forward (shopping cart, uphill, cycling); pulses normal, unlike vascular claudication Ankylosing spondylitis SpondyloarthritisThe familySeronegative spondyloarthritis (PAIR: psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, reactive arthritis, formerly Reiter syndrome) shares human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27), enthesitis and anterior uveitis. Ankylosing spondylitis also brings aortic regurgitation (aortitis), stiffens the chest wall (restrictive lung disease), may scar the upper lobes, and thins bone. Its mimic, diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, affects an older man with flowing ossification over 4 or more vertebrae and normal sacroiliac joints; it is not spondyloarthritis. Man, most often aged 20 to 40; morning stiffness that eases with use; night pain Insidious, over 3 months; sacroiliitis on imaging Vertebral metastasis Batson plexusRouteProstate cancer reaches the lumbar spine through the vertebral (Batson) venous plexus, often as osteoblastic lesions. Prior cancer (prostate, breast, kidney, thyroid, lung); weight loss Weeks, worsening; night pain that no position or analgesic relieves; MRI with contrast Vertebral osteomyelitis Injection drug use, hemodialysis or bacteremia; focal tenderness Continuous pain; fever often absent; ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein) high; MRI Vertebral compression fracture Older, osteoporosis or chronic glucocorticoids; a minor fall or lift Sudden; point tenderness over one vertebra; radiograph first Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment

Course of low back pain Under 4 to 6 weeksNo imaging without a red flag; most recover Past 6 weeksRadicular pain or a deficit: MRI (the ladder, rung 2) Over 3 months, onset by 40Inflammatory back pain

Inflammatory versus mechanical back pain Feature Inflammatory Mechanical Onset By age 40, gradual, over 3 months Any age, often sudden after an event Night Wakes the patient; eases on getting up Usually absent Morning stiffness Marked, eases with use Brief Rest and activity Worse with rest, better with exercise Better with rest

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any low back pain → Red-flag history and a neurologic exam No red flag, exam normal, under 4 to 6 weeks No imaging: treat Bladder, saddle or upper motor neuron signs Emergent MRI Any other red flag Image by cause, below Targeted tests TestResultMeans Prior cancer, night pain, weight loss → MRI of the spine with contrast MRI not possible CT, or a radiograph with ESR or CRP Lesion Metastasis Fever, injection drug use, bacteremia → MRI; blood cultures, ESR and CRP Infected vertebra Vertebral osteomyelitis Epidural collection Spinal epidural abscess Older, osteoporosis, minor trauma → Radiograph Collapsed vertebra Compression fracture Inflammatory pattern → Sacroiliac joint radiographs Sacroiliitis Ankylosing spondylitis Radiographs normal, suspicion still high MRI of the sacroiliac joints SkipImaging for acute pain with no red flag; rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (spondyloarthritis is seronegative) unless peripheral arthritis suggests another diagnosis; HLA-B27 as proof. HLA-B27HLA-B27Human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27) is present in about 90% of White patients with ankylosing spondylitis but also in up to 10% of the general population, so it supports the diagnosis and rarely makes it.

Acute low back pain: start on the lowest rung not yet tried Rung Do Move on when 1 An NSAID or acetaminophen; stay active; a nonbenzodiazepine muscle relaxant second line Still painful at 4 to 6 weeks, or a new red flag 2 Physical therapy and exercise Radicular pain past 6 weeks: MRI 3 Epidural glucocorticoid injection, severe or persistent radicular pain Conservative care fails 4 Surgical referral Cauda equina, or an unequivocal disc herniation with a progressive deficit or intractable pain after 6 weeks

Treatment by cause Cause Treatment Ankylosing spondylitis An NSAID and daily exercise, then a TNF (tumor necrosis factor) or IL-17 (interleukin-17) inhibitor Beyond the NSAIDSecond lineMethotrexate and sulfasalazine help only peripheral arthritis. Blocking TNF impairs granulomas and can reactivate latent tuberculosis. Malignant spinal cord compression Dexamethasone, then decompression, or radiation for a radiosensitive tumor

briefs.sub: four categories by mechanism, not appearance · cold shock in children · perfusion before pressure · septic shock ladderIs perfusion abnormal, and what is wrong with the circulation rather than with the skin?
blocks: four categories by mechanism, not appearance · cold shock in children · perfusion before pressure · septic shock ladderIs perfusion abnormal, and what is wrong with the circulation rather than with the skin?

Pt 4 yo F, fever to 40 C, petechial rash, obtundation, capillary refill 4 seconds, no response to three fluid boluses; no blood pressure reported Q the category of shock; options spanned distributive, cardiogenic, hypovolemic and obstructive

Fever, a petechial rash and shock in a preschooler indicate septic shock. Septic shock is by definition distributive. Inflammatory mediators produce vasodilation and capillary leak, so blood is maldistributed rather than absent, inadequate or obstructed. She does not look vasodilated. Capillary refill of 4 seconds is cold shock, which is how children usually present. Children compensate by vasoconstricting and raising the heart rate, so the bedside picture mimics hypovolemia. The vignette gives no blood pressure, because in children hypotension is a late, pre-arrest finding.

Distributive shock vasodilation and capillary leak with maldistributed flow despite normal or high cardiac output Shock in a child a perfusion diagnosis: mental status, capillary refill above 2 seconds, weak pulses, urine output under 1 mL/kg/h Hypotension not required, and marks decompensation when present Fluid-refractory shock persistent after 40 to 60 mL/kg, the trigger to start a vasoactive infusion

For puffy eyes in a child, decide first whether the swelling is confined to the eye or spread over the whole child. If it is generalized, the urinalysis sorts it: protein alone means nephrotic syndrome, and blood with high blood pressure means nephritis.

Salient decoyPuffiness worst in the morning in an allergic child, treated as allergy without a urine dipstick. Mirror twinPSGN also starts with puffy eyes; blood in the urine and a high blood pressure separate it. What it is An inflammatory syndrome of proximal aching and stiffness in adults over 50, without true weakness, closely tied to giant cell arteritis Driver Likely low-grade synovitis and bursitis around the girdles, not muscle injury, so the CK stays normal Triggers Age over 50 (non-modifiable) Female sex, about 2 to 1 (non-modifiable) Chain Inflammation: girdle bursitis and synovitis ESR and C-reactive protein (CRP) rise Clinical: shoulder and hip girdle aching morning stiffness over an hour pain limits movement while strength stays normal Insights Pain, not weakness, keeps the patient in bed: true weakness with a high CK points to myositis The steroid response is part of the diagnosis: relief comes in hours to days on low-dose prednisone, and no response by a week points elsewhere

Who age over 50 Pain bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching, morning stiffness over 60 minutes, normal strength Labs ESR raised, usually over 50; CRP raised; CK normal Response dramatic improvement on low-dose prednisone within days

Giant cell arteritisNew headache, jaw claudication, vision loss or amaurosis fugax; untreated, a high risk of blindness, higher with jaw claudication or diplopia; about half of patients with arteritis also have polymyalgia rheumatica If it is suspected, choose high-dose glucocorticoids at once, without waiting for the biopsy; consider IV pulse first if vision is impaired; the temporal artery biopsy follows. BiopsyTemporal artery biopsyThe arteritis is segmental, so the biopsy takes a long segment, and a negative biopsy does not exclude it. Treatment is not delayed for it: the biopsy can be done up to 2 weeks after glucocorticoids start. Jaw claudication and diplopia carry a higher risk of blindness.
